source.title: RAGChecker: A Fine-grained Framework for Diagnosing Retrieval-Augmented Generation

claims.summary: Authors identify two evaluation challenges: RAG is modular (retriever plus generator) so metrics must assess the whole system and each module; and existing metrics such as recall@k/MRR depend on annotated chunks and rigid chunking, while n-gram metrics for generators are coarse-grained.
Authors state that the reliability of existing RAG metrics, i.e. their alignment with human judgments, remains under-explored.

RAGChecker is based on claim-level entailment checking: claims are extracted from the response and the ground-truth answer and checked against other texts; it outputs overall metrics, diagnostic retriever metrics, and diagnostic generator metrics.

Author claim: compared with RAGAS, TruLens and ARES (fine-grained only on some metrics) and RGB, RECALL, NoMIRACL (specific aspects), all RAGChecker metrics are claim-level and designed to give actionable insights into error sources.

The framework targets two personae: a user who wants a single metric to rank systems, and a developer who needs to find causes of mistakes. Response errors are classified as retrieval errors (retriever fails to return complete and relevant context) or generator errors (generator fails to identify and leverage relevant information in context).
A modular RAG system is formulated as RAG = {R, G}: the retriever returns top-k chunks for query q from documents D, and the generator produces response m from those chunks and q.

Two components enable fine-grained evaluation: a text-to-claim extractor that decomposes text into claims, and a claim-entailment checker that decides whether a claim is entailed by a reference text. A response may contain correct claims, incorrect claims, and miss ground-truth claims.

claims.summary: Overall metrics: precision is the proportion of response claims entailed by the ground-truth answer; recall is the proportion of ground-truth claims entailed by the response; F1 is their harmonic mean.

Retriever metrics: claim recall is the proportion of ground-truth claims entailed by the retrieved chunks; context precision is chunk-level, the number of relevant chunks (chunks entailing at least one ground-truth claim) divided by k.

Because a fixed-size chunk can contain both relevant and irrelevant or misleading information, even the best retriever would score below 100% on a claim-level precision; the authors therefore define precision at chunk level for interpretability.
Faithfulness is the proportion of response claims entailed by the retrieved chunks; higher is better.

Incorrect response claims are split three ways: entailed by a relevant chunk (relevant noise sensitivity), entailed by an irrelevant chunk (irrelevant noise sensitivity), or not entailed by any retrieved chunk (hallucination); each is a proportion of all response claims.
Self-knowledge is the proportion of correct response claims not entailed by any chunk; a lower score is better only when the generator is expected to depend fully on retrieved context.

Context utilization is the number of ground-truth claims that are entailed by the retrieved chunks and also by the response, divided by the number of ground-truth claims entailed by the retrieved chunks; higher is generally preferred.

Appendix B gives complete formulas: relevant/irrelevant chunks are assigned by ground-truth claim entailment, and all generator noise, hallucination and self-knowledge metrics share the denominator of all response claims.
claims.section: B The complete formula for all metrics

claims.summary: Eight RAG systems are evaluated: 2 retrievers (BM25 sparse, E5-Mistral dense) times 4 generators (GPT-4, Mixtral-8x7B, Llama3-8B, Llama3-70B). Llama3-70B is used as both claim extractor and checker via RefChecker.
The benchmark contains 4,162 queries across 10 domains, repurposed from public open-domain QA datasets, with short answers converted to long-form answers.

claims.summary: Default setup: 300-token chunks with overlap ratio 0.2, top-20 chunks as context, temperature 0.0; GPT-4 is gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09 and E5-Mistral is e5-mistral-7b-instruct.
claims.section: D Details of the Experiment Setup

claims.summary: The meta evaluation dataset has 280 pairwise instances (10 domains x 28 system pairs); each pair is labeled by two annotators on correctness, completeness and overall assessment with a five-level relative preference.
Ten annotators (seven in-house, three graduate students) labeled the meta evaluation; the annotation UI showed GPT-4-generated critiques comparing each response with the ground truth.

Author-stated limitations: retriever metrics are less insightful than generator metrics; metrics do not distinguish Neutral from Contradiction checking results; the benchmark is English, text-only and repurposed from existing datasets.
Author observation: among generator metrics, context utilization correlates strongly with overall F1, and context utilization is relatively stable across the two retrievers.
Author interpretation: generators show chunk-level faithfulness, trusting a relevant chunk as a whole while an irrelevant chunk has minimal impact.
Author observation: open-source generators are faithful but tend to trust context blindly, especially when retrieval improves; GPT-4 has higher context utilization and lower noise sensitivity.

Appendix F diagnosis setup: three systems (BM25_GPT-4, E5-Mistral_GPT-4, E5-Mistral_Llama3-70B) on three domains (Writing, Finance, KIWI), varying k in {5,10,20}, chunk size {150,300,600}, overlap {0.0,0.2,0.4}, and generation prompts.
claims.section: F Diagnosis on RAG for Improvements

claims.summary: Author observation from Appendix F: larger k lowers context precision while larger chunk size raises it, but both raise claim recall; more context tends to raise faithfulness while context utilization worsens and relevant noise sensitivity rises.

claims.summary: Author observation: higher chunk overlap generally raised context precision but did not consistently change other metrics, so overlap may not need extensive tuning.

claims.summary: Authors note a risk that developers may optimize for RAGChecker's specific metrics at the expense of broader utility, and that quantitative measures can neglect user experience.
Authors argue generator-only evaluations with manually constructed datasets cannot reveal how generation results are entangled with retrieval behavior.
Overall assessment Pearson correlation with human preference: RAGChecker 61.93, best baseline RAGAS Answer Similarity 48.31, human annotator correlation 70.09.
